title: Biryani By Kilo's Sealed Handi Delivery Takes the Struggle Out of Dum Biryani
excerpt: India's largest dum biryani chain delivers every order in the same earthen pot it's cooked in, complete with a candle-powered reheating kit that ensures the seal-breaking moment is worth the wait.
body:
• Biryani By Kilo delivers each biryani in a sealed handi (earthen pot) with an angeethi reheating kit, preserving the dum cooking flavors until the customer breaks the seal
  • The chain operates over 100 company-owned outlets across 45+ cities in India, with every order freshly cooked and delivered within 90 minutes
  • BBK sources its handis from artisans in Kumhaara Gram on the outskirts of Delhi, supporting traditional potters while maintaining its signature presentation
  • Founded in 2015 by IIT alumni, the brand has grown into a Rs 400-crore business that has made the sealed handi a cultural ritual for biryani lovers

The Handi Problem Every Biryani Lover Knows

Anyone who has ordered a dum biryani in a sealed handi knows the struggle: the dough seal is stubbornly tight, the pot is blazing hot, and cracking it open without sending rice flying requires a combination of patience and technique that most hungry diners simply do not possess. It is the price of authenticity — the very seal that traps the steam and spices during dum cooking becomes an obstacle course at the dinner table.

Biryani By Kilo, India's largest dum-cooked biryani chain, has turned this common frustration into a feature. Every order arrives in the same clay handi in which it was cooked, sealed with dough just as it would be in a traditional kitchen. But the chain has refined the experience so thoroughly that breaking the seal has become a ritual rather than a chore — and the drama of the steam release is now half the reason people order.

How the Handi System Works

The process begins in BBK's kitchen the moment an order is placed. Spices sourced directly from vendors in Kerala are mixed in precise quantities by VKL Seasonings and packed in pre-portioned pouches. Two-year aged Daawat basmati rice, the same grade used by five-star restaurants, goes into individual clay handis along with in-house butchered meat. The handi is sealed with dough and placed on dum — slow-cooked for 35 to 40 minutes until the flavors are locked inside.

The sealed pot is then delivered as-is to the customer, accompanied by a small earthen bowl (an angeethi or makeshift hearth) and candles. The instructions are simple: light the candles, place the handi on the bowl, wait eight to ten minutes, and then break the seal. The result is a rush of fragrant steam and a biryani that tastes as if it just came off the fire.

"The quality of rice we use is used by five-star restaurants like Dumpukht or Bukhara. Other chains use the Rs 70-80 per kg rice that has been aged in three months unnaturally."

— Vishal Jindal, Co-founder and CEO, Biryani By Kilo

From IIT Classroom to 100 Outlets

Biryani By Kilo was founded in 2015 in Gurugram by Vishal Jindal and Kaushik Roy, both IIT alumni who saw an opportunity in India's fragmented biryani market. The market, estimated at close to $4 billion according to a Technopak study, was dominated by unorganized local players with no consistency in quality or hygiene. BBK's bet was that a standardized, premium product delivered with theatrical flair could command higher prices and build loyalty.

That bet has paid off. The chain now operates more than 100 company-owned outlets across 45-plus cities, deliberately avoiding the franchise model to maintain quality control. Average order values hover around Rs 1,000 — significantly higher than most competitors — and more than 75 percent of orders come through online channels. The company has grown into a roughly Rs 400-crore business and continues to expand, with plans for a presence in the Middle East and Far East.

The Artisan Supply Chain

One of the quieter aspects of BBK's model is its sourcing of the handis themselves. The chain buys its clay pots from Kumhaara Gram, a potters' village on the outskirts of Delhi. The arrangement cuts out middlemen and provides steady employment to traditional craftsmen and artisans who might otherwise struggle to find markets for their work.

The supply chain extends across India. Spices come from Kerala, meat is processed in-house to control cuts and quality, and the rice is the same two-year naturally aged Daawat basmati used by luxury hotel restaurants. Every outlet follows Standard Operating Procedures to ensure that a biryani in Kolkata tastes the same as one in Bengaluru.

Why It Resonates With the Diaspora

For Indian Americans and NRIs who grew up with the ritual of dum biryani — the sealed pot, the communal breaking of the seal, the first aromatic burst — BBK's model taps into deep food memories. While the chain has not yet expanded to the United States, its approach has influenced how Indian restaurants worldwide think about biryani presentation and delivery. The sealed handi has become a benchmark: if it does not arrive sealed, it probably was not dum-cooked to order.

BBK offers three standard variants at all times — Hyderabadi, Lucknowi, and Kolkata — and rotates limited-edition styles like Malabar and Ambur biryani. The dessert menu includes Matka Phirni, served in its own small earthen pot, extending the clay-vessel presentation across the meal.

What Comes Next

The company has signaled international ambitions, with discussions underway with food and beverage partners in the Middle East and Far East. Whether the handi-and-candle experience translates across cultures remains to be seen, but in India the model has proven that biryani can be both a premium product and a delivery-friendly one — as long as you are willing to wait eight minutes before you eat.
